findings.where: Article specimen: the title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law', at both widths
findings.fault: The article title is set in a heavy, tightly spaced bold serif. The tile's own type spec gives Newsreader only three weights: Light 300 for display, 400 for reading and 500 for subheads. It has no bold. So the title is in a weight outside the system. It also reads in a different voice from the light, open hero line. The two largest serif lines on the site are Mark's statement and an article title, and they are treated as if they came from two different publications. At a glance the title is the darkest, loudest thing below the fold.
findings.who_objects: The founder and Mark. The direction promises a refined legal journal with a light, high-contrast serif (Freshfields F10), and the brief asks for refined, serious type. A heavy black headline on every article page pulls toward a news-tabloid tone. It also tells Angélique there is no single title style to follow when she adds articles.

findings.where: Motion sketch: the 'Replay the entrance' button and the timing table's figures ('0 ms', '150 ms', '1050 ms'), at both widths
findings.fault: This sans text looks letter-spaced wider than the same Public Sans elsewhere, for example 'Write to Mark' in the hero strip and the palette labels. The tile's type note says Public Sans is never tracked. The one button on the page and the table's numbers sit loose next to the rest of the label type, so like parts are not treated alike.
findings.who_objects: Whoever turns this tile into the site's styles. The spec and the render disagree, so they would not know which is the rule. A careful reader comparing the hero's address label with the button would also see two sans settings with no reason for the difference.

findings.where: Motion sketch: the easing curve drawn in the framed diagram, at both widths
findings.fault: The curve is drawn in the logo blue. The palette states that blue is kept for the wordmark, links and focus. Here it marks a static graphic that cannot be acted on, so the page's one link colour appears on something that is not a link.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader of the tile, and the founder judging whether the palette holds to its own roles. The tile states a strict rule for blue and then breaks it in its own specimen. That weakens the promise that blue always means 'you can act on this'.
